# Recap and lecture overview 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Brief recap of last class
### Early computing and data representation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 27px;"}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Computers went from [people]{.alert} to mechanical calculators to silicon chips
- The [Von Neumann architecture]{.alert} keeps instructions and data in one memory
- Everything is stored in [binary]{.alert}, base 2, using only 0s and 1s
- One digit is a [bit]{.alert}. Eight bits are a [byte]{.alert}
- [Hexadecimal]{.alert} is base 16, and one hex digit covers exactly four bits
- [Abstraction]{.alert} is what lets numbers stand for images and text
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
[![](figures/hexadecimal.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/hexadecimal.png"}
:::
:::
:::

## Brief recap of last class
### Representing images, colours and text

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 27px;"}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- An image is a grid of [pixels]{.alert}
- [RGB]{.alert} gives each pixel three numbers from 0 to 255: red, green, and blue
- That is 8 bits per channel, so [16.7 million colours]{.alert}
- Text is split into characters, and each character gets a number
- [ASCII]{.alert} is a lookup table for 128 characters
- [Unicode]{.alert} extends it to accents, other alphabets, and emoji
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
[![](figures/rgb.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/rgb.png"}
:::
:::
:::

## Brief recap of last class
### Programming languages

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 27px;"}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- [Konrad Zuse]{.alert} built the first programmable computers in the 1940s
- [Assembly]{.alert} gives machine code readable names, one line per instruction
- [Low-level languages]{.alert} are fast, but hard to read and write
- [High-level languages]{.alert} like Python hide the hardware and run anywhere
- [Compiled]{.alert} languages translate first. [Interpreted]{.alert} ones translate as they run
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="margin-top: -20px;"}
[![](figures/high-low-languages.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/high-low-languages.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

# What is the command line? 💻 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## A computer in a nutshell
### Operating system

:::{style="font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Source: Dave Kerr](figures/kernel-and-user-space.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/kernel-and-user-space.png"}
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- The [operating system]{.alert} sits between your programs and the hardware, and manages access to it
- It has two halves: the [kernel]{.alert} and [user space]{.alert}
- The [kernel]{.alert} talks to the hardware, runs the drivers, and hands out memory and CPU time
- Code running in the kernel can break everything, which is why [users are kept out of it]{.alert}
- [User space]{.alert} is where your programs run, each in its own sandbox, asking the kernel for whatever it needs
- Curiosity: the Linux kernel source is [on GitHub](https://github.com/torvalds/linux)
:::
:::
:::

## A computer in a nutshell
### Kernels and shells

:::{style="font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Source: Dave Kerr](figures/kernel-and-user-space.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/kernel-and-user-space.png"}
[![](figures/walnut.jpeg){width="25%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/walnut.jpeg"}
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- A [shell]{.alert} is a user space program that lets you reach the system's resources
- Use it [interactively]{.alert} by typing at a terminal, or run a [script]{.alert}, a file full of commands
- Most people use a [graphical interface]{.alert} instead. Same idea, prettier surface
- [Why "kernel" and "shell"?]{.alert} A nut has a soft kernel protected by a hard shell. Useful metaphor, _innit_?
:::
:::
:::

## Interacting with the shell
### Terminals

:::{style="font-size: 25px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Source: Dave Kerr](figures/diagram3-terminal-and-shell.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/diagram3-terminal-and-shell.png"}
:::
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- You never talk to the shell directly. You talk to a [terminal]{.alert}
- A terminal [reads your keystrokes]{.alert}, passes them to a program, and [shows the results]{.alert}
- A shell cannot do that on its own. It needs a terminal as its interface
- [Why "terminal"?]{.alert} Before screens, a [terminal was hardware](https://www.friendlywire.com/articles/vintage-computers/): a keyboard wired to a [mainframe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainframe_computer), often many terminals to one machine
- Working on a data centre or cloud machine today is much the same, with a nicer screen 😉
:::
:::
:::

## Interacting with the shell
### Command line

:::{style="font-size: 25px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Source: Dave Kerr](figures/diagram3-terminal-and-shell.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/diagram3-terminal-and-shell.png"}
:::
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- A terminal is simply a [text-based interface]{.alert}. The first thing it does is start a shell
- The shell takes input two ways: [interactively]{.alert} from the command line, or from a [script]{.alert}
- It sends output back to the terminal, or to a file
- The [command line]{.alert} is the line you type on. You can [customise it](https://ohmyz.sh/) with colours and shortcuts
:::
:::
:::

## Shell variants
### Bash, Zsh, and others

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
[![](figures/runningbashscript.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/runningbashscript.png"}
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- There are [many shells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_command_shells), and they differ in what they can do
- [bash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bash_(Unix_shell)) is the default on most Unix-like systems. The name stands for Bourne-Again Shell
- [zsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z_shell) is the default on macOS
- Windows has [cmd.exe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cmd.exe) and [PowerShell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerShell). There is also [C Shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_shell), and many more
- Your terminal starts your preferred shell automatically, and you can [change which one](https://effective-shell.com/part-1-transitioning-to-the-shell/getting-started/)
:::
:::
:::

## Why bother with the shell?
### The programmer's best friend

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 30px;"}
:::{.incremental}
1. [Speed.]{.alert} Typing beats hunting through menus with a mouse

2. [Power.]{.alert} Some things simply cannot be done from a graphical interface

3. [Reproducibility.]{.alert} A script can be run again. Clicking cannot

4. [Portability.]{.alert} The same commands work on your laptop, a [Raspberry Pi](https://www.raspberrypi.com/), or a supercomputer

5. [Automation.]{.alert} Shells are programmable, so repetitive work becomes a script

6. [Employability.]{.alert} Servers, containers, and cloud tools all run on Linux, which is why [the shell is having a renaissance](https://effective-shell.com/part-1-transitioning-to-the-shell/the-renaissance-of-the-shell/)
:::
:::

# The Unix philosophy {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## The Unix philosophy

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 25px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="55%"}
- Our tools come from [Unix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix), built at Bell Labs in the 1970s
- They still follow the [Unix philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_philosophy):

> **Do One Thing And Do It Well**

- Each tool is small and does a single job
- Chain the small tools together and you can build something large
- Hence the description: [minimalist and modular]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width="45%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Unix Version 5, 1974. The home directories `ken` and `dmr` belong to Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie](figures/unix-v5.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/unix-v5.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Things to use the shell for

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 32px;"}
:::{.incremental}
- [Find and navigate files]{.alert} faster than any file browser
- [Rename and move files in bulk]{.alert}, hundreds at a time
- [Version control with Git]{.alert}, which is where most Git commands live
- [Install and update software]{.alert} with a single command
- [Connect to remote machines]{.alert} over SSH, including cloud servers
- [Run jobs on supercomputers]{.alert}, which often offer nothing but a shell
:::
:::

# Shell basics 🐚 🤓 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Shell: First look

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}

Let's open up our shell!

Click on the **View** menu, then **Terminal**. You can also use the shortcut ``Ctrl + ` `` (backtick).

## Shell: First look

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 27px;"}
You should see something like:

```bash
$  username@hostname:~$
```

This is shell-speak for: "Who am I and where am I?" 

- `username` denotes a specific user (one of potentially many on this computer).

- `@hostname` denotes the name of the computer or server.

- `:~` denotes the directory path (where `~` signifies the user's home directory).

- `$` (or maybe `%`) denotes the start of the command prompt.

    - (For a special "superuser" called root, the dollar sign will change to a `#`).

```bash
$ whoami
$ pwd

dafreir
/Users/dafreir/Documents/github/datasci350/lectures/lecture-03
```
:::

# Syntax {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Syntax

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
All bash commands have the same basic syntax:

[**command option(s) argument(s)**]{.alert}

**Examples:**

```bash
$ # list files in the Documents directory 
$ # in long format and human-readable sizes
$
$ ls -lh ~/Documents 
```

<br>

```bash
$ # sort the file and display 
$ # only unique lines
$
$ sort -u file.txt 
```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
[Commands]{.alert}

- You don't always need options or arguments

- For example:
  - `ls ~/Documents/` and `ls -lh ~/Documents` are both valid commands that will yield (different) output

- However, you always need a command!
:::
:::
:::

## Syntax

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
All Bash commands have the same basic syntax:

command [option(s)]{.alert} argument(s)

**Examples:**

```bash
$ # list files in the Documents directory 
$ # in long format and human-readable sizes
$
$ ls -lh ~/Documents 
```

<br>

```bash
$ # sort the file and display 
$ # only unique lines
$
$ sort -u file.txt 
```
:::

:::{.column style="width: 40%; font-size: 22px;"}
[Options]{.alert} (also called [flags]{.alert})

- Start with a dash, usually one letter
- Chain several under a single dash

```bash
$ ls -l -a -h /var/log  # this works
$ ls -lah /var/log      # so does this
```

- Longer, spelled-out names take two dashes

:::{style="font-size: 24px;"}
```bash
$ ls --human-readable /var/log
```
:::

- `-l` long listing, `-a` all files including hidden ones, `-h` readable sizes
- `-u` on `sort` keeps only unique lines
- Hard to remember what each letter means? [You're totally right!]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::

## Syntax

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
All Bash commands have the same basic syntax:

command option(s) [argument(s)]{.alert}

**Examples:** 

```bash
$ # list files in the Documents directory 
$ # with human-readable sizes
$ ls -lh ~/Documents/
```

<br>

```bash
$ # sort the file and remove duplicates
$ sort -u file.txt
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[Arguments]{.alert}

-   Tell the command *what* to operate on

-   What counts as a valid argument depends on the command

-   Can be a file, path, a set of files and folders, a string, and more

-   Sometimes more than just one argument is needed:

```bash
$ mv figs/cat.png best-figs/cat02.png
```
:::
:::
:::

# Help! 🆘 😟 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Multiple ways to get help

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- `man ls` opens the manual page for `ls`. Press `q` to quit

- Manual pages come in numbered sections. Run `man man` to see them

- [`cht.sh`](https://cht.sh/) gives short, practical answers straight in the terminal (you may need to [install `curl`](https://curl.se/download.html) first):

```bash
$ curl cht.sh/ls
```

:::{style="text-align: center"}
[![](figures/chtsh.png){width="70%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/chtsh.png"}
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[![](figures/beatles-help.jpeg){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/beatles-help.jpeg"}

- Or you can use an LLM (or Google) to search for help on a command 
- There's a great chance that someone else has already asked the same question you have 😉
:::
:::
:::

## Multiple ways to get help

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- You can also install the `tldr` tool ([GitHub repository](https://github.com/tldr-pages/tldr)) which provides simplified help pages for common commands. Run it like this: `tldr command`

```bash
$ tldr ls

Successfully updated local database

ls

List directory contents.
More information: <https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/ls-invocation.html>.

- List files one per line:
    ls -1

- List all files, including hidden files:
    ls [-a|--all]

- List files with a trailing symbol to indicate file type (directory/, symbolic_link@, executable*, ...):
    ls [-F|--classify]

... (the manual continues; press q to quit)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[![](figures/beatles-help.jpeg){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/beatles-help.jpeg"}

- For more info on how to get help, see [here](https://effective-shell.com/part-1-transitioning-to-the-shell/getting-help/)
:::
:::
:::

## Getting help with `man`

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}

The `man` command ("manual pages") is your friend if you need help

```bash
$ man ls

LS(1)               General Commands Manual          LS(1)

NAME
     ls – list directory contents

SYNOPSIS
     ls [-@ABCFGHILOPRSTUWabcdefghiklmnopqrstuvwxy1%,] [--color=when]
    [-D format] [file ...]

DESCRIPTION
     For each operand that names a file of a type other than directory, ls
     displays its name as well as any requested, associated information.  For
     each operand that names a file of type directory, ls displays the names
     of files contained within that directory, as well as any requested,
     associated information.

     If no operands are given, the contents of the current directory are
     displayed.  If more than one operand is given, non-directory operands are

... (the manual continues; press q to quit)
```

:::

## Getting help with `man`

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
`man` shows the page in a [pager]{.alert}, a small viewer for long text. The keys you need:

- `j` and `k`, or the arrow keys, move one line
- `d` and `u` move half a page, `space` and `b` a whole one
- `g` and `G` jump to the very start and the very end
- `/pattern` searches forwards, `?pattern` backwards. Then `n` and `N` for the next and previous hit
- `q` quits
- `h` lists every other key
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/rtfm-bayeux.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/rtfm-bayeux.png"}
[RTFM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RTFM)! 😂

**Always check the documentation!**
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Navigating your file system 🧭 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Navigating your file system

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{.incremental}
- Phones and tablets hide the file system from you completely
- In data science you need to find your way around it quickly
- The questions that keep coming up:
  - Where am I right now?
  - Where is my home directory?
  - Where are my files, and where do I want to put them?
  - How do I get from here to there?
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[![](figures/that-way-giphy.gif){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/that-way-giphy.gif"}
:::
:::
:::

## Navigation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
Key navigation commands are:

- `pwd` to print (the current) working directory
- `cd` to change directory

```bash
$ pwd

/Users/dafreir/Documents/github/datasci350/lectures/lecture-03
```

Paths can be [absolute]{.alert} (from the top) or [relative]{.alert} (from where you are). Prefer relative ones, and use these shortcuts:

- `~` your home folder
- `.` the current directory
- `..` the directory above
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{.fragment .fade-in}

Let's try it out!

Accessing the `figures/` directory:

```bash
$ # mkdir figures # Create a directory called figures (if it doesn't exist)
$ cd figures # Change to the figures directory
$ pwd

/Users/dafreir/Documents/github/datasci350/lectures/lecture-03/figures
```

Now, let's go back to the previous directory:

```bash
$ cd ../ # Go back to the previous directory
$ pwd

/Users/dafreir/Documents/github/datasci350/lectures/lecture-03
```

Back two directories:

```bash
$ cd ../../ # Go back two directories
$ pwd

/Users/dafreir/Documents/github/datasci350
```
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Navigation

:::{style="font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
Beware of spaces in names. Say you have a folder called "My Documents" (I'm looking at you, Windows)

- `cd My Documents` fails. Bash reads `My` and `Documents` as two separate arguments
- Two ways around it:
  - Quote the name: `cd "My Documents"`
  - Escape the space: `cd My\ Documents`. Tab completion does this for you
- Better still: [never put spaces in names]{.alert}
- Use lowercase with dashes or underscores, like `assignment-05` or `assignment_05`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 40px;"}
[![](figures/expanding-brain.jpg){width="60%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/expanding-brain.jpg"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## More navigation commands: A cheat sheet

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
[Getting around]{.alert}

| Command | What it does |
|:--|:--|
| `pwd` | Print the working directory |
| `cd dir` | Change directory |
| `cd -` | Back to where you just were |
| `ls` | List files here |
| `ls -l` | Long format, with details |
| `ls -a` | Include hidden files |
| `ls -lh` | Long format, readable sizes |
| `ls -R` | Include subdirectories |
| `~` `.` `..` | Home, here, one level up |
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
[Working with files]{.alert}

| Command | What it does |
|:--|:--|
| `mkdir` | Create a directory |
| `touch` | Create an empty file |
| `cp` | Copy |
| `mv` | Move, or rename |
| `rm` | Delete a file. No undo! |
| `rmdir` | Delete an empty directory |
| `cat` | Show what is in a file |
| `find` | Search for files |

A fuller list is [here](https://effective-shell.com/part-1-transitioning-to-the-shell/navigating-your-system/)
:::
:::
:::

## Shell navigation exercise

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
Type each command. Look at the result before you move on

1. Go to your home directory: `cd ~`
2. Create a directory and enter it: `mkdir practice && cd practice`
3. Create two empty files: `touch file1.txt file2.txt`
4. List the contents: `ls`
5. Rename `file2.txt` to `file3.txt`: `mv file2.txt file3.txt`
6. List again to check, then go home: `ls && cd ~`
7. [Warning]{.alert}: `rm -rf` deletes at once, with no Trash and no undo. Read the path, then delete the directory: `rm -rf practice`
8. Check that it is gone: `ls`
:::

## Shell navigation exercise to try at home

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}  
1. Go to your home directory: `cd ~`
2. Create a directory: `mkdir shell-practice`
3. Enter it: `cd shell-practice`
4. Create three empty files: `touch file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt`
5. List the contents: `ls`
6. Create a subdirectory: `mkdir subdir`
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
7. Move a file into it: `mv file2.txt subdir/`
8. Copy a file: `cp file1.txt file4.txt`
9. List everything, subdirectory included: `ls -R`
10. Go up one level: `cd ..`
11. [Warning]{.alert}: the next command deletes the folder and everything inside it. Check the name, then run `rm -r shell-practice`
12. Check that it is gone: `ls`

Bonus: use `man` to read about any command you used.

- Which commands surprised you?
- Which did you find most useful?
:::
:::
:::

## Summary
### Today we...

:::{style="margin-top:40px; font-size: 28px;"}
:::{.incremental}
- The [shell]{.alert} runs your commands. The [terminal]{.alert} is the window you type them in
- Every command has the same shape: `command [options] arguments`
- Options are short (`-l`) or spelled out (`--human-readable`), and they combine: `ls -lah`
- `pwd` says where you are, `ls` shows what is there, `cd` moves you
- `~` is home, `.` is here, `..` is one level up
- `man`, `tldr`, and `cht.sh` answer your questions. `q` gets you out of the pager
- The [Unix philosophy]{.alert}: small tools that each do one thing, combined to do big things
:::
:::
